problem: Implicit-memory ObjectNav methods struggle with long-term memory and planning, while explicit map methods (2D semantic grids, VLFM value maps) have few categories, lack fine-grained semantics, or are target-specific and non-reusable.
motivation: ObjectNav needs long-horizon scene understanding, memory of visited areas and semantic priors. A compact explicit memory that keeps rich visual/text features lets a VLM reason efficiently without processing entire image histories.
key_idea: Build an online Frontier-Object map with geometric, distance, visual (DINOv2) and text features for frontiers and 3D objects, feed them as tokens to a LLaVA-style LLM that picks the next frontier or object goal, and execute it with A*+FMM, trained on automatically generated navigation data.
insight: Localized frontier image features matter much more than global ones (Table 1: (c)->(g) +5.3 SR / +5.7 SPL), and object image and text features are complementary. Training data collected with automatic segmentation matters more than GT-segmentation data despite being smaller, since it closes the train/inference gap. Segmentation quality is the main bottleneck: GT masks give 86.6 SR / 56.1 SPL vs 75.8 / 47.9 with automatic ones.
method: Obstacle mapping: back-project depth into a 5cm-voxel scene point cloud, project to a 2D obstacle/exploration map with inflation, and extract frontiers (VLFM/Yamauchi style)

Object mapping: Mask2Former (fine-tuned per benchmark) instance masks are back-projected, DBSCAN-filtered, and merged into 3D object clouds when point overlap exceeds 50% at 3cm, with weighted-averaged category distributions and DINOv2 features

Frontier/object/path tokens: frontier tokens sum MLP embeddings of endpoints, center, localized DINOv2 mask feature and geodesic (FMM) distance; object tokens add 3D center, bbox corners, distance, DINOv2 feature and CLIP text category; path tokens encode past 2D locations; each has a learnable type embedding

LLM goal predictor: LLaVA-v1.6 7B (frozen LLM, trained encoders and head) with a prompt asking where to go to find the target category; a binary head chooses frontier vs object, then a bilinear similarity E_N^T A^T A E picks the specific goal (loss BCE + 0.5 CE)

Low-level planner: FMM distance map used as heuristic for A*, plus a collision map; if the goal object is unexplored the agent goes to the nearest frontier, otherwise to a computed stopping area; the episode starts with a 360° rotation

Automatic dataset: in Habitat on HM3D/MP3D, the expert picks the visible target object, else the frontier minimizing the average distance to agent and to GT stopping points; collected with GT and automatic segmentation (760k steps on HM3D)

setting.backbone: LLaVA-v1.6 7B (LLM frozen, MLP encoders and prediction head trained) + Mask2Former + DINOv2 + CLIP text encoder; Llama 3.2 1B for OVON
setting.training_data: Self-generated trajectories from HM3D (145 scenes; 490k GT-seg + 270k auto-seg steps) and MP3D (50 scenes; 215k + 80k steps); Mask2Former fine-tuned on 2000 images per training house; OVON: 610k+362k steps over all HM3D categories
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D 640x480 with camera pose from external SLAM/simulator
setting.action_space: discrete: forward 25cm, turn ±30°, stop (high-level goals are frontiers/objects, executed by A*+FMM)
setting.privileged: Camera pose assumed given (GT pose in sim); GT annotations only in training data generation; single-floor episodes only in main comparison; 2D distance for success on HM3D v2

results: FOM-Nav reaches 75.8 SR / 47.9 SPL on HM3D v2, beating the best VLFM variant (60.3/33.6, VLFM* 64.0/33.0) and PIRLNav (66.0/27.0). It has the highest SPL on all single-floor and full benchmarks, though SR is lower than implicit methods on cross-floor and MP3D episodes.
limitations: Cannot handle multi-floor navigation (stairs are obstacles), so implicit methods win on cross-floor episodes
Performance bottlenecked by instance segmentation quality (11.0 SR drop from GT masks); needs external pose and per-benchmark segmentation training
Open-vocabulary generalization is limited because the encoders and head are trained from scratch, lacking Internet-scale pretraining
